pgrp.summary: Returns the permutation group generated by the permutations p_1, ..., p_k.
pgrp.body_md:
Returns the permutation group generated by the permutations `p_1`, ..., `p_k`.

Calling forms:

- `pgrp(p_1, ..., p_k)`
- `pgrp([p_1, ..., p_k])`: the same, with the generators in one list

The generators may be `pgrp_perm` values or lists of images, of any degrees; the group's degree is the largest. A group displays as `pgrp(degree n, k generators)`.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) S4 : pgrp(pgrp_from_cycles([[1, 2]]), pgrp_from_cycles([[1, 2, 3, 4]]));
(%o1) pgrp(degree 4, 2 generators)
(%i2) pgrp_order(S4);
(%o2) 24
```

See also: `pgrp_generators`, `pgrp_subgroup`

pgrp_abelian_groups.summary: Returns every abelian group of order n, as lists of invariant factors.
pgrp_abelian_groups.body_md:
Returns every abelian group of order `n`, as lists of invariant factors.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) pgrp_abelian_groups(36);
(%o1) [[2, 18], [3, 12], [6, 6], [36]]
```

See also: `pgrp_abelian_invariants`

pgrp_abelian_invariants.summary: Returns the invariant factors [d_1, d_2, ...] of an abelian group G, with each d_i dividing the next.
pgrp_abelian_invariants.body_md:
Returns the invariant factors [d_1, d_2, ...] of an abelian group `G`, with each d_i dividing the next.

`G` is isomorphic to Z_d1 x Z_d2 x .... The trivial group gives `[]`. Fails if `G` isn't abelian.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) pgrp_abelian_invariants(pgrp_direct_product(pgrp_cyclic(4), pgrp_cyclic(6)));
(%o1) [2, 12]
```

See also: `pgrp_abelian_groups`, `pgrp_abelian_p`

pgrp_abelian_p.summary: Returns true if G is abelian.
pgrp_abelian_p.body_md:
Returns `true` if `G` is abelian.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) [pgrp_abelian_p(pgrp_cyclic(6)), pgrp_abelian_p(pgrp_symmetric(3))];
(%o1) [true, false]
```

See also: `pgrp_cyclic_p`, `pgrp_centre`

pgrp_action_perm.summary: Returns the permutation of points that one element g induces through act.
pgrp_action_perm.body_md:
Returns the permutation of `points` that one element `g` induces through `act`.

Point `i` goes to the position of `act(g, points[i])` in `points`.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) X : [[0, 1], [1, 0], [1, 1]]$
(%i2) act : lambda([m, v], map(lambda([t], mod(t, 2)), list_matrix_entries(m . transpose(matrix(v)))))$
(%i3) pgrp_action_perm(matrix([1, 1], [0, 1]), X, act);
(%o3) (1 3)
```

See also: `pgrp_from_action`

examples.input: act : lambda([m, v], map(lambda([t], mod(t, 2)), list_matrix_entries(m . transpose(matrix(v)))))$

pgrp_alternating.summary: Returns the alternating group A_n, the even permutations of 1, ..., n.
pgrp_alternating.body_md:
Returns the alternating group A_n, the even permutations of 1, ..., n.

It is generated by the 3-cycles (1 2 k) for k = 3, ..., n.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) [pgrp_order(pgrp_alternating(5)), pgrp_simple_p(pgrp_alternating(5))];
(%o1) [60, true]
```

See also: `pgrp_symmetric`, `pgrp_sign`

pgrp_apply.summary: Returns the image of the point i under the permutation p.
pgrp_apply.body_md:
Returns the image of the point `i` under the permutation `p`.

Points beyond the degree of `p` are fixed.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) p : pgrp_from_cycles([[1, 2, 3]])$
(%i2) makelist(pgrp_apply(p, i), i, 1, 5);
(%o2) [2, 3, 1, 4, 5]
```

See also: `pgrp_perm_list`, `pgrp_support`

pgrp_cayley_table.summary: Returns the Cayley table of a group, or of a list of permutations, as a matrix.
pgrp_cayley_table.body_md:
Returns the Cayley table of a group, or of a list of permutations, as a matrix.

Calling forms:

- `pgrp_cayley_table(G)`: the elements of `G` in `pgrp_elements` order, labelled 1, 2, ...
- `pgrp_cayley_table(l)`: the permutations in the list `l`, labelled 1, 2, ...
- `pgrp_cayley_table(G, labels)`, `pgrp_cayley_table(l, labels)`: with the labels given

Row a, column b holds a∘b. Fails if a list isn't closed under composition.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) pgrp_cayley_table(pgrp_cyclic(3), ["e", "r", "r^2"]);
      [  ∘    e    r   r^2 ]
      [                    ]
      [  e    e    r   r^2 ]
(%o1) [                    ]
      [  r    r   r^2   e  ]
      [                    ]
      [ r^2  r^2   e    r  ]
```

See also: `pgrp_elements`, `pgrp_compose`

examples.input:
pgrp_cayley_table(pgrp_cyclic(3), ["e", "r", "r^2"]);
      [  ∘    e    r   r^2 ]
      [                    ]
      [  e    e    r   r^2 ]

pgrp_centraliser.summary: Returns the centraliser C_G(A), the elements of G that commute with every permutation in A.
pgrp_centraliser.body_md:
Returns the centraliser C_G(A), the elements of `G` that commute with every permutation in `A`.

`A` is a list of permutations or a group.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) pgrp_elements(pgrp_centraliser(pgrp_symmetric(4), [pgrp_from_cycles([[1, 2]], 4)]));
(%o1) [(), (3 4), (1 2), (1 2)(3 4)]
```

See also: `pgrp_centre`, `pgrp_normaliser`

pgrp_centre.summary: Returns the centre Z(G), the elements that commute with every element of G.
pgrp_centre.body_md:
Returns the centre Z(G), the elements that commute with every element of `G`.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) pgrp_elements(pgrp_centre(pgrp_dihedral(4)));
(%o1) [(), (1 3)(2 4)]
```

See also: `pgrp_centraliser`, `pgrp_abelian_p`

pgrp_colouring_orbits.summary: Returns one colouring from each orbit of G on the colourings of its points with colours 1, ..., k.
pgrp_colouring_orbits.body_md:
Returns one colouring from each orbit of `G` on the colourings of its points with colours 1, ..., `k`.

A colouring is a list whose entry `i` is the colour of point `i`; it is not a permutation. Each colouring returned is the least in its orbit, and there are `pgrp_count_orbits(G, k)` of them. `G` moves a colouring by carrying the colour at point i to point g(i).

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) pgrp_colouring_orbits(pgrp_dihedral(4), 2);
(%o1) [[1, 1, 1, 1], [1, 1, 1, 2], [1, 1, 2, 2], [1, 2, 1, 2], [1, 2, 2, 2], [2, 2, 2, 2]]
```

See also: `pgrp_count_orbits`

pgrp_commutator.summary: Returns the commutator [x, y] = x^-1 y^-1 x y.
pgrp_commutator.body_md:
Returns the commutator [x, y] = x^-1 y^-1 x y.

It is the identity exactly when `x` and `y` commute.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) [pgrp_commutator(pgrp_from_cycles([[1, 2]], 3), pgrp_from_cycles([[2, 3]])),
       pgrp_commutator(pgrp_from_cycles([[1, 2]], 4), pgrp_from_cycles([[3, 4]]))];
(%o1) [(1 3 2), ()]
```

See also: `pgrp_derived_subgroup`, `pgrp_conjugate`

pgrp_compose.summary: Composes permutations right to left: pgrp_compose(s, t) applies t first, then s.
pgrp_compose.body_md:
Composes permutations right to left: `pgrp_compose(s, t)` applies `t` first, then `s`.

This is s∘t in Dummit and Foote's notation. With more arguments, `pgrp_compose(a, b, c)` is a∘b∘c, so `c` applies first. Permutations of different degrees are padded with fixed points. The examples are D&F's products (1 2 3)∘(1 2)(3 4) = (1 3 4) and (1 2)∘(1 3) = (1 3 2).

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) pgrp_compose(pgrp_from_cycles([[1, 2, 3]]), pgrp_from_cycles([[1, 2], [3, 4]]));
(%o1) (1 3 4)
(%i2) pgrp_compose(pgrp_from_cycles([[1, 2]]), pgrp_from_cycles([[1, 3]]));
(%o2) (1 3 2)
```

See also: `pgrp_inverse`, `pgrp_power`

pgrp_composition_series.summary: Returns a composition series G = G_0 > G_1 > ... > 1, each a normal subgroup of the one before with a simple quotient.
pgrp_composition_series.body_md:
Returns a composition series G = G_0 > G_1 > ... > 1, each a normal subgroup of the one before with a simple quotient.

Each step takes a largest proper normal subgroup, which lists elements, so keep `G` small.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) map(pgrp_order, pgrp_composition_series(pgrp_symmetric(4)));
(%o1) [24, 12, 4, 2, 1]
```

See also: `pgrp_simple_p`, `pgrp_quotient`

pgrp_conjugacy_class.summary: Returns the conjugacy class of x in G, every g x g^-1 for g in G.
pgrp_conjugacy_class.body_md:
Returns the conjugacy class of `x` in `G`, every g x g^-1 for g in `G`.

In A_4 the eight 3-cycles split into two classes of four.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) pgrp_conjugacy_class(pgrp_alternating(4), pgrp_from_cycles([[1, 2, 3]], 4));
(%o1) [(2 4 3), (1 2 3), (1 3 4), (1 4 2)]
```

See also: `pgrp_conjugacy_classes`, `pgrp_conjugate`

pgrp_conjugacy_classes.summary: Returns the conjugacy classes of G, with the identity's first.
pgrp_conjugacy_classes.body_md:
Returns the conjugacy classes of `G`, with the identity's first.

Each class is sorted, and the classes come in order of their least elements.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) pgrp_conjugacy_classes(pgrp_symmetric(3));
(%o1) [[()], [(2 3), (1 2), (1 3)], [(1 2 3), (1 3 2)]]
```

See also: `pgrp_conjugacy_class`, `pgrp_conjugate`

pgrp_conjugate.summary: Returns the conjugate g x g^-1.
pgrp_conjugate.body_md:
Returns the conjugate g x g^-1.

Conjugating relabels the points: if `x` has the cycle (a b c), then g x g^-1 has the cycle (g(a) g(b) g(c)). In the example g = (1 3)(2 4 5) relabels (1 2 3) as (3 4 1), which is (1 3 4).

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) pgrp_conjugate(pgrp_from_cycles([[1, 2, 3]], 5), pgrp_from_cycles([[1, 3], [2, 4, 5]]));
(%o1) (1 3 4)
```

See also: `pgrp_conjugacy_class`, `pgrp_commutator`

pgrp_count_orbits.summary: Counts the colourings of the points of G with k colours, counting two as the same when an element of G turns one into the other.
pgrp_count_orbits.body_md:
Counts the colourings of the points of `G` with `k` colours, counting two as the same when an element of `G` turns one into the other.

This is Burnside's lemma: the average over `G` of k^c(g), where c(g) is the number of cycles of g, fixed points included. `k` may be a symbol, which gives a polynomial. The example colours the faces of a cube, labelled 1 up, 2 down, 3 front, 4 right, 5 back, 6 left.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) cube : pgrp(pgrp_from_cycles([[3, 4, 5, 6]]), pgrp_from_cycles([[1, 4, 2, 6]]))$
(%i2) display2d : false$
(%i3) [pgrp_count_orbits(cube, 3), expand(pgrp_count_orbits(cube, k))];
(%o3) [57,k^6/24+k^4/8+k^3/2+k^2/3]
```

See also: `pgrp_cycle_index`, `pgrp_colouring_orbits`

pgrp_cycle_index.summary: Returns the cycle index of G as a polynomial in x[1], x[2], ...
pgrp_cycle_index.body_md:
Returns the cycle index of `G` as a polynomial in `x[1]`, `x[2]`, ...

Calling forms:

- `pgrp_cycle_index(G)`: in `x[1]`, `x[2]`, ...
- `pgrp_cycle_index(G, y)`: in `y[1]`, `y[2]`, ...

It averages x[1]^m_1 x[2]^m_2 ... over `G`, where m_j is the number of j-cycles. Substituting x[j] = r^j + b^j counts colourings by how often each colour is used (Pólya's theorem).

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) display2d : false$
(%i2) Z : pgrp_cycle_index(pgrp_cyclic(4));
(%o2) (2*x[4]+x[2]^2+x[1]^4)/4
(%i3) expand(subst(makelist(x[j] = r^j + b^j, j, 1, 4), Z));
(%o3) r^4+b*r^3+2*b^2*r^2+b^3*r+b^4
```

See also: `pgrp_count_orbits`

pgrp_cycle_type.summary: Returns the lengths of the cycles of p, fixed points included, largest first.
pgrp_cycle_type.body_md:
Returns the lengths of the cycles of `p`, fixed points included, largest first.

The lengths add up to the degree of `p`.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) pgrp_cycle_type(pgrp_from_cycles([[1, 2]], 5));
(%o1) [2, 1, 1, 1]
```

See also: `pgrp_cycles`, `pgrp_element_order`

pgrp_cycles.summary: Returns the disjoint cycles of p as lists, leaving out fixed points.
pgrp_cycles.body_md:
Returns the disjoint cycles of `p` as lists, leaving out fixed points.

Each cycle starts at its least point, and the cycles come in order of their least points. The identity gives `[]`. The example is D&F's permutation of 1, ..., 13 from §1.3.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) pgrp_cycles(pgrp_perm([12, 13, 3, 1, 11, 9, 5, 10, 6, 4, 7, 8, 2]));
(%o1) [[1, 12, 8, 10, 4], [2, 13], [5, 11, 7], [6, 9]]
```

See also: `pgrp_from_cycles`, `pgrp_cycle_type`

pgrp_cyclic.summary: Returns the cyclic group Z_n, generated by (1 2 ... n).
pgrp_cyclic.body_md:
Returns the cyclic group Z_n, generated by (1 2 ... n).

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) Z6 : pgrp_cyclic(6)$
(%i2) [pgrp_order(Z6), pgrp_generators(Z6)];
(%o2) [6, [(1 2 3 4 5 6)]]
```

See also: `pgrp_cyclic_p`, `pgrp_dihedral`

pgrp_cyclic_p.summary: Returns true if G is cyclic.
pgrp_cyclic_p.body_md:
Returns `true` if `G` is cyclic.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) [pgrp_cyclic_p(pgrp_direct_product(pgrp_cyclic(2), pgrp_cyclic(3))), pgrp_cyclic_p(pgrp_direct_product(pgrp_cyclic(2), pgrp_cyclic(2)))];
(%o1) [true, false]
```

See also: `pgrp_abelian_p`, `pgrp_cyclic`

pgrp_degree.summary: Returns the number of points a group or a permutation acts on.
pgrp_degree.body_md:
Returns the number of points a group or a permutation acts on.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) [pgrp_degree(pgrp_dihedral(5)), pgrp_degree(pgrp_from_cycles([[1, 2]], 4)), pgrp_degree([2, 1, 3])];
(%o1) [5, 4, 3]
```

See also: `pgrp_order`

pgrp_derived_series.summary: Returns the derived series G, G', G'', ..., until it stops getting smaller.
pgrp_derived_series.body_md:
Returns the derived series G, G', G'', ..., until it stops getting smaller.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) map(pgrp_order, pgrp_derived_series(pgrp_symmetric(4)));
(%o1) [24, 12, 4, 1]
```

See also: `pgrp_derived_subgroup`, `pgrp_solvable_p`

pgrp_derived_subgroup.summary: Returns the derived subgroup G' = [G, G], generated by all commutators.
pgrp_derived_subgroup.body_md:
Returns the derived subgroup G' = [G, G], generated by all commutators.

It is the smallest normal subgroup with an abelian quotient.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) pgrp_isomorphic_p(pgrp_derived_subgroup(pgrp_symmetric(4)), pgrp_alternating(4));
(%o1) true
```

See also: `pgrp_derived_series`, `pgrp_commutator`

pgrp_dihedral.summary: Returns the dihedral group D_2n of order 2n, the symmetries of a regular n-gon.
pgrp_dihedral.body_md:
Returns the dihedral group D_2n of order 2n, the symmetries of a regular n-gon.

The vertices are 1, ..., n in order. The generators are r = (1 2 ... n), the rotation sending i to i + 1, and s, the reflection fixing vertex 1, as in Dummit and Foote §1.2. `n` must be at least 3.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) D8 : pgrp_dihedral(4)$
(%i2) [pgrp_order(D8), pgrp_generators(D8)];
(%o2) [8, [(1 2 3 4), (2 4)]]
```

See also: `pgrp_cyclic`, `pgrp_symmetric`

pgrp_direct_product.summary: Returns the direct product G x H, with G on the first points and H on the points after them.
pgrp_direct_product.body_md:
Returns the direct product G x H, with `G` on the first points and `H` on the points after them.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) P : pgrp_direct_product(pgrp_cyclic(2), pgrp_cyclic(3))$
(%i2) [pgrp_degree(P), pgrp_order(P), pgrp_generators(P)];
(%o2) [5, 6, [(1 2), (3 4 5)]]
```

See also: `pgrp_abelian_invariants`

pgrp_element_order.summary: Returns the order of p, the least k at least 1 with p^k the identity.
pgrp_element_order.body_md:
Returns the order of `p`, the least `k` at least 1 with `p^k` the identity.

It is the least common multiple of the cycle lengths.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) pgrp_element_order(pgrp_from_cycles([[1, 2], [3, 4, 5], [6, 7, 8, 9]]));
(%o1) 12
```

See also: `pgrp_cycle_type`, `pgrp_order_profile`

pgrp_elements.summary: Returns every element of G, in order of their lists of images.
pgrp_elements.body_md:
Returns every element of `G`, in order of their lists of images.

Fails for groups with more than `pgrp_max_elements` elements.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) pgrp_elements(pgrp_symmetric(3));
(%o1) [(), (2 3), (1 2), (1 2 3), (1 3 2), (1 3)]
```

See also: `pgrp_order`, `pgrp_max_elements`

pgrp_eq.summary: Returns true if p and q are the same permutation, whatever their degrees.
pgrp_eq.body_md:
Returns `true` if `p` and `q` are the same permutation, whatever their degrees.

`=` also compares degrees, so (1 2) of degree 2 and (1 2) of degree 3 are different under `=` and equal under `pgrp_eq`. A shorter permutation counts as fixing the extra points. Either argument may be a list of images.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) a : pgrp_perm([2, 1])$
(%i2) b : pgrp_perm([2, 1, 3])$
(%i3) [is(a = b), pgrp_eq(a, b), pgrp_eq(a, [2, 1, 3, 4])];
(%o3) [false, true, true]
```

See also: `pgrp_perm`, `pgrp_sort`

pgrp_fixed_points.summary: Returns the points that p leaves where they are, in increasing order.
pgrp_fixed_points.body_md:
Returns the points that `p` leaves where they are, in increasing order.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) pgrp_fixed_points(pgrp_from_cycles([[2, 4]], 5));
(%o1) [1, 3, 5]
```

See also: `pgrp_support`, `pgrp_count_orbits`

pgrp_from_action.summary: Returns the permutation group that gens induce on the list points through act(g, x).
pgrp_from_action.body_md:
Returns the permutation group that `gens` induce on the list `points` through `act(g, x)`.

Point `i` stands for `points[i]`. `gens` can be matrices, permutations or anything `act` accepts, and `act(g, x)` must return an element of `points`. In the example, GL_2(F_2) acts on the three nonzero vectors of F_2^2 as S_3.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) X : [[0, 1], [1, 0], [1, 1]]$
(%i2) act : lambda([m, v], map(lambda([t], mod(t, 2)), list_matrix_entries(m . transpose(matrix(v)))))$
(%i3) G : pgrp_from_action([matrix([1, 1], [0, 1]), matrix([0, 1], [1, 0])], X, act)$
(%i4) [pgrp_order(G), pgrp_isomorphic_p(G, pgrp_symmetric(3))];
(%o4) [6, true]
```

See also: `pgrp_action_perm`, `pgrp_orbit`

examples.input: act : lambda([m, v], map(lambda([t], mod(t, 2)), list_matrix_entries(m . transpose(matrix(v)))))$

pgrp_from_cycles.summary: Builds a permutation from a list of cycles, read as a product right to left.
pgrp_from_cycles.body_md:
Builds a permutation from a list of cycles, read as a product right to left.

Calling forms:

- `pgrp_from_cycles(cycles)`: the degree is the largest point in the cycles
- `pgrp_from_cycles(cycles, n)`: degree `n`

The cycles need not be disjoint: `pgrp_from_cycles([[1, 2], [1, 3]])` is (1 2)∘(1 3).

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) pgrp_from_cycles([[1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]);
(%o1) (1 2)(3 4 5)
(%i2) pgrp_from_cycles([[1, 2], [1, 3]]);
(%o2) (1 3 2)
(%i3) pgrp_degree(pgrp_from_cycles([[1, 2]], 5));
(%o3) 5
```

See also: `pgrp_cycles`, `pgrp_perm`

pgrp_generators.summary: Returns the generators of G, padded to its degree.
pgrp_generators.body_md:
Returns the generators of `G`, padded to its degree.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) pgrp_generators(pgrp(pgrp_from_cycles([[1, 2]]), pgrp_from_cycles([[3, 4]])));
(%o1) [(1 2), (3 4)]
```

See also: `pgrp`

pgrp_hom.summary: Returns the homomorphism from G to H that sends the generators of G to images.
pgrp_hom.body_md:
Returns the homomorphism from `G` to `H` that sends the generators of `G` to `images`.

`images` lists one element of `H` for each element of `pgrp_generators(G)`, in that order. Fails if no homomorphism does that. A homomorphism displays as `pgrp_hom(degree m to degree n)`. The example squares in Z_4.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) Z4 : pgrp_cyclic(4)$
(%i2) sq : pgrp_hom(Z4, Z4, [pgrp_power(first(pgrp_generators(Z4)), 2)]);
(%o2) pgrp_hom(degree 4 to degree 4)
(%i3) pgrp_elements(pgrp_kernel(sq));
(%o3) [(), (1 3)(2 4)]
```

See also: `pgrp_hom_apply`, `pgrp_kernel`, `pgrp_image`

pgrp_hom_apply.summary: Returns the image of the permutation p under the homomorphism phi.
pgrp_hom_apply.body_md:
Returns the image of the permutation `p` under the homomorphism `phi`.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) sgn : pgrp_sign_hom(pgrp_symmetric(4))$
(%i2) [pgrp_hom_apply(sgn, pgrp_from_cycles([[1, 2]], 4)), pgrp_hom_apply(sgn, pgrp_from_cycles([[1, 2, 3]], 4))];
(%o2) [(1 2), ()]
```

See also: `pgrp_hom`

pgrp_hom_p.summary: Returns true if x is a homomorphism.
pgrp_hom_p.body_md:
Returns `true` if `x` is a homomorphism.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) [pgrp_hom_p(pgrp_sign_hom(pgrp_symmetric(3))), pgrp_hom_p(pgrp_symmetric(3))];
(%o1) [true, false]
```

See also: `pgrp_hom`, `pgrp_p`

pgrp_identity.summary: Returns the identity permutation of degree n.
pgrp_identity.body_md:
Returns the identity permutation of degree `n`.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) [pgrp_identity(4), pgrp_degree(pgrp_identity(4))];
(%o1) [(), 4]
```

See also: `pgrp_perm`

pgrp_image.summary: Returns the image of phi, a subgroup of its target.
pgrp_image.body_md:
Returns the image of `phi`, a subgroup of its target.

By the first isomorphism theorem, the orders of the kernel and the image multiply to the order of the source.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) sgn : pgrp_sign_hom(pgrp_symmetric(4))$
(%i2) [pgrp_order(pgrp_image(sgn)), pgrp_order(pgrp_kernel(sgn)) * pgrp_order(pgrp_image(sgn))];
(%o2) [2, 24]
```

See also: `pgrp_kernel`

pgrp_index.summary: Returns the index [G : H], the number of cosets of H in G.
pgrp_index.body_md:
Returns the index [G : H], the number of cosets of `H` in `G`.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) pgrp_index(pgrp_symmetric(4), pgrp_dihedral(4));
(%o1) 3
```

See also: `pgrp_left_cosets`

pgrp_inverse.summary: Returns the inverse of the permutation p.
pgrp_inverse.body_md:
Returns the inverse of the permutation `p`.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) pgrp_inverse(pgrp_from_cycles([[1, 2, 3, 4]]));
(%o1) (1 4 3 2)
```

See also: `pgrp_compose`, `pgrp_power`

pgrp_isomorphic_p.summary: Returns true if G and H are isomorphic.
pgrp_isomorphic_p.body_md:
Returns `true` if `G` and `H` are isomorphic.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) [pgrp_isomorphic_p(pgrp_dihedral(3), pgrp_symmetric(3)), pgrp_isomorphic_p(pgrp_dihedral(4), pgrp_quaternion())];
(%o1) [true, false]
```

See also: `pgrp_isomorphism`, `pgrp_order_profile`

pgrp_isomorphism.summary: Returns an isomorphism from G to H, or false if there is none.
pgrp_isomorphism.body_md:
Returns an isomorphism from `G` to `H`, or `false` if there is none.

It compares invariants first, then searches for images of the generators. In the example the isomorphism from Z_6 to Z_2 x Z_3 sends the 6-cycle to a 2-cycle times a 3-cycle, and Z_4 is not isomorphic to the Klein four-group.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) iso : pgrp_isomorphism(pgrp_cyclic(6), pgrp_direct_product(pgrp_cyclic(2), pgrp_cyclic(3)))$
(%i2) pgrp_hom_apply(iso, pgrp_from_cycles([[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]]));
(%o2) (1 2)(3 4 5)
(%i3) pgrp_isomorphism(pgrp_cyclic(4), pgrp(pgrp_from_cycles([[1, 2], [3, 4]]), pgrp_from_cycles([[1, 3], [2, 4]])));
(%o3) false
```

See also: `pgrp_isomorphic_p`

pgrp_kernel.summary: Returns the kernel of phi, the subgroup of its source that it sends to the identity.
pgrp_kernel.body_md:
Returns the kernel of `phi`, the subgroup of its source that it sends to the identity.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) K : pgrp_kernel(pgrp_sign_hom(pgrp_symmetric(4)))$
(%i2) [pgrp_order(K), pgrp_isomorphic_p(K, pgrp_alternating(4))];
(%o2) [12, true]
```

See also: `pgrp_image`, `pgrp_preimage`

pgrp_left_cosets.summary: Returns the left cosets gH of H in G.
pgrp_left_cosets.body_md:
Returns the left cosets gH of `H` in `G`.

Each coset is sorted, and the cosets come in order of their least elements, so two such lists are equal exactly when the cosets are.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) pgrp_left_cosets(pgrp_symmetric(3), pgrp(pgrp_from_cycles([[1, 2]], 3)));
(%o1) [[(), (1 2)], [(2 3), (1 3 2)], [(1 2 3), (1 3)]]
```

See also: `pgrp_right_cosets`, `pgrp_index`, `pgrp_quotient`

pgrp_lower_central_series.summary: Returns the lower central series G, [G, G], [[G, G], G], ..., until it stops getting smaller.
pgrp_lower_central_series.body_md:
Returns the lower central series G, [G, G], [[G, G], G], ..., until it stops getting smaller.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) map(pgrp_order, pgrp_lower_central_series(pgrp_dihedral(8)));
(%o1) [16, 4, 2, 1]
```

See also: `pgrp_nilpotent_p`, `pgrp_derived_series`

pgrp_max_elements.summary: Default value: 100000. The largest group that the functions which list elements will handle.
pgrp_max_elements.body_md:
Default value: 100000. The largest group that the functions which list elements will handle.

Most structure functions work by listing a group's elements, so they refuse larger groups. `pgrp_order`, `pgrp_member_p`, `pgrp_orbits` and `pgrp_stabiliser_chain` don't list elements and work on any size.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) pgrp_max_elements : 100$
(%i2) errcatch(pgrp_elements(pgrp_symmetric(5)));
pgrp_elements: the group has 120 elements, more than pgrp_max_elements = 100
(%o2) []
```

See also: `pgrp_elements`, `pgrp_order`

examples.input:
errcatch(pgrp_elements(pgrp_symmetric(5)));
pgrp_elements: the group has 120 elements, more than pgrp_max_elements = 100

pgrp_member_p.summary: Returns true if the permutation p is in G.
pgrp_member_p.body_md:
Returns `true` if the permutation `p` is in `G`.

Like `pgrp_order`, it works on groups too big to list.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) A4 : pgrp_alternating(4)$
(%i2) [pgrp_member_p(A4, pgrp_from_cycles([[1, 2, 3]])), pgrp_member_p(A4, pgrp_from_cycles([[1, 2]]))];
(%o2) [true, false]
```

See also: `pgrp_subgroup_p`

pgrp_nilpotent_p.summary: Returns true if the lower central series of G reaches the trivial group.
pgrp_nilpotent_p.body_md:
Returns `true` if the lower central series of `G` reaches the trivial group.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) [pgrp_nilpotent_p(pgrp_dihedral(4)), pgrp_nilpotent_p(pgrp_symmetric(3))];
(%o1) [true, false]
```

See also: `pgrp_lower_central_series`, `pgrp_solvable_p`

pgrp_normal_closure.summary: Returns the smallest normal subgroup of G that contains S, a list of permutations or a group.
pgrp_normal_closure.body_md:
Returns the smallest normal subgroup of `G` that contains `S`, a list of permutations or a group.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) pgrp_elements(pgrp_normal_closure(pgrp_symmetric(4), [pgrp_from_cycles([[1, 2], [3, 4]])]));
(%o1) [(), (1 2)(3 4), (1 3)(2 4), (1 4)(2 3)]
```

See also: `pgrp_normal_subgroups`

pgrp_normal_p.summary: Returns true if H is a normal subgroup of G.
pgrp_normal_p.body_md:
Returns `true` if `H` is a normal subgroup of `G`.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) S4 : pgrp_symmetric(4)$
(%i2) [pgrp_normal_p(pgrp_alternating(4), S4), pgrp_normal_p(pgrp(pgrp_from_cycles([[1, 2]])), S4)];
(%o2) [true, false]
```

See also: `pgrp_subgroup_p`, `pgrp_normal_subgroups`

pgrp_normal_subgroups.summary: Returns every normal subgroup of G, smallest first.
pgrp_normal_subgroups.body_md:
Returns every normal subgroup of `G`, smallest first.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) map(pgrp_order, pgrp_normal_subgroups(pgrp_symmetric(4)));
(%o1) [1, 4, 12, 24]
```

See also: `pgrp_subgroups`, `pgrp_normal_p`, `pgrp_simple_p`

pgrp_normaliser.summary: Returns the normaliser N_G(H), the elements g of G with g H g^-1 = H.
pgrp_normaliser.body_md:
Returns the normaliser N_G(H), the elements g of `G` with g H g^-1 = H.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) S4 : pgrp_symmetric(4)$
(%i2) pgrp_elements(pgrp_normaliser(S4, pgrp_subgroup(S4, [pgrp_from_cycles([[1, 2]], 4)])));
(%o2) [(), (3 4), (1 2), (1 2)(3 4)]
```

See also: `pgrp_centraliser`, `pgrp_normal_p`

pgrp_orbit.summary: Returns the orbit of the point x under G, sorted.
pgrp_orbit.body_md:
Returns the orbit of the point `x` under `G`, sorted.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) pgrp_orbit(pgrp(pgrp_from_cycles([[1, 2]]), pgrp_from_cycles([[3, 4, 5]])), 4);
(%o1) [3, 4, 5]
```

See also: `pgrp_orbits`, `pgrp_stabiliser`

pgrp_orbits.summary: Returns the orbits of G on its points, each sorted, in order of their least points.
pgrp_orbits.body_md:
Returns the orbits of `G` on its points, each sorted, in order of their least points.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) pgrp_orbits(pgrp(pgrp_from_cycles([[1, 2]]), pgrp_from_cycles([[3, 4, 5]])));
(%o1) [[1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]
```

See also: `pgrp_orbit`, `pgrp_stabiliser`

pgrp_order.summary: Returns the number of elements of G.
pgrp_order.body_md:
Returns the number of elements of `G`.

It doesn't list the elements, so it works on groups far too big to list.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) pgrp_order(pgrp_symmetric(20));
(%o1) 2432902008176640000
```

See also: `pgrp_elements`, `pgrp_stabiliser_chain`

pgrp_order_profile.summary: Returns how many elements of G have each order, as [order, count] pairs.
pgrp_order_profile.body_md:
Returns how many elements of `G` have each order, as `[order, count]` pairs.

Isomorphic groups have the same profile, so a difference shows two groups are not isomorphic. D_8 and Q_8 differ in their elements of order 2.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) [pgrp_order_profile(pgrp_dihedral(4)), pgrp_order_profile(pgrp_quaternion())];
(%o1) [[[1, 1], [2, 5], [4, 2]], [[1, 1], [2, 1], [4, 6]]]
```

See also: `pgrp_isomorphic_p`, `pgrp_element_order`

pgrp_p.summary: Returns true if x is a permutation group.
pgrp_p.body_md:
Returns `true` if `x` is a permutation group.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) [pgrp_p(pgrp_symmetric(3)), pgrp_p(pgrp_perm([2, 1]))];
(%o1) [true, false]
```

See also: `pgrp_perm_p`, `pgrp_hom_p`

pgrp_perm.summary: Turns a list of images into a permutation value.
pgrp_perm.body_md:
Turns a list of images into a permutation value.

Entry `i` of `l` is the image of `i`. The value keeps the degree `length(l)`. `string(p)` gives `pgrp_perm([...])`, which reads back as the same value, and `tex(p)` gives the cycles.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) p : pgrp_perm([2, 3, 1, 4]);
(%o1) (1 2 3)
(%i2) pgrp_degree(p);
(%o2) 4
(%i3) is(p = pgrp_from_cycles([[1, 2, 3]], 4));
(%o3) true
(%i4) string(p);
(%o4) pgrp_perm([2,3,1,4])
```

See also: `pgrp_perm_list`, `pgrp_from_cycles`, `pgrp_perm_p`

pgrp_perm_list.summary: Returns the list of images of the permutation p.
pgrp_perm_list.body_md:
Returns the list of images of the permutation `p`.

Calling forms:

- `pgrp_perm_list(p)`: the images, one for each point up to the degree of `p`
- `pgrp_perm_list(p, n)`: padded with fixed points to length `n`; fails if `p` moves a point above `n`

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) p : pgrp_from_cycles([[1, 3]]);
(%o1) (1 3)
(%i2) pgrp_perm_list(p);
(%o2) [3, 2, 1]
(%i3) pgrp_perm_list(p, 5);
(%o3) [3, 2, 1, 4, 5]
```

See also: `pgrp_perm`, `pgrp_apply`

pgrp_perm_output.summary: Default value: true. When true, functions return permutations as pgrp_perm values; when false, they return lists of images.
pgrp_perm_output.body_md:
Default value: `true`. When `true`, functions return permutations as `pgrp_perm` values; when `false`, they return lists of images.

Colourings and lists of invariant factors are lists either way, since they are not permutations.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) pgrp_compose([2, 3, 1], [2, 1, 3]);
(%o1) (1 3)
(%i2) pgrp_perm_output : false$
(%i3) pgrp_compose([2, 3, 1], [2, 1, 3]);
(%o3) [3, 2, 1]
```

See also: `pgrp_perm`, `pgrp_perm_list`

pgrp_perm_p.summary: Returns true if x is a permutation value, and false for anything else, including a list of images.
pgrp_perm_p.body_md:
Returns `true` if `x` is a permutation value, and `false` for anything else, including a list of images.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) [pgrp_perm_p(pgrp_perm([2, 1])), pgrp_perm_p([2, 1])];
(%o1) [true, false]
```

See also: `pgrp_perm`

pgrp_power.summary: Returns p composed with itself k times.
pgrp_power.body_md:
Returns `p` composed with itself `k` times.

`k` may be zero or negative.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) r : pgrp_from_cycles([[1, 2, 3, 4]])$
(%i2) [pgrp_power(r, 2), pgrp_power(r, 4), pgrp_power(r, -1)];
(%o2) [(1 3)(2 4), (), (1 4 3 2)]
```

See also: `pgrp_compose`, `pgrp_element_order`

pgrp_preimage.summary: Returns the elements of the source that phi sends into the subgroup K of its target.
pgrp_preimage.body_md:
Returns the elements of the source that `phi` sends into the subgroup `K` of its target.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) sgn : pgrp_sign_hom(pgrp_symmetric(3))$
(%i2) pgrp_elements(pgrp_preimage(sgn, pgrp(pgrp_identity(2))));
(%o2) [(), (1 2 3), (1 3 2)]
```

See also: `pgrp_kernel`, `pgrp_image`

pgrp_quaternion.summary: Returns the quaternion group Q_8, acting on itself by left multiplication.
pgrp_quaternion.body_md:
Returns the quaternion group Q_8, acting on itself by left multiplication.

Points 1, ..., 8 stand for 1, -1, i, -i, j, -j, k, -k, and the generators are i and j. An element g sends the point 1 to the point that names g.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) Q8 : pgrp_quaternion()$
(%i2) [pgrp_order(Q8), pgrp_order_profile(Q8)];
(%o2) [8, [[1, 1], [2, 1], [4, 6]]]
```

See also: `pgrp_dihedral`, `pgrp_isomorphic_p`

pgrp_quotient.summary: Returns the quotient G/N of G by a normal subgroup N, as G acting on the left cosets of N.
pgrp_quotient.body_md:
Returns the quotient G/N of `G` by a normal subgroup `N`, as `G` acting on the left cosets of `N`.

Point `i` stands for the `i`-th coset of `pgrp_left_cosets(G, N)`.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) S4 : pgrp_symmetric(4)$
(%i2) V4 : pgrp(pgrp_from_cycles([[1, 2], [3, 4]]), pgrp_from_cycles([[1, 3], [2, 4]]))$
(%i3) Q : pgrp_quotient(S4, V4)$
(%i4) [pgrp_order(Q), pgrp_isomorphic_p(Q, pgrp_symmetric(3))];
(%o4) [6, true]
```

See also: `pgrp_quotient_hom`, `pgrp_left_cosets`

pgrp_quotient_hom.summary: Returns the homomorphism from G onto pgrp_quotient(G, N) that sends g to its coset gN.
pgrp_quotient_hom.body_md:
Returns the homomorphism from `G` onto `pgrp_quotient(G, N)` that sends g to its coset gN.

Its kernel is `N`.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) S4 : pgrp_symmetric(4)$
(%i2) V4 : pgrp(pgrp_from_cycles([[1, 2], [3, 4]]), pgrp_from_cycles([[1, 3], [2, 4]]))$
(%i3) q : pgrp_quotient_hom(S4, V4)$
(%i4) [pgrp_order(pgrp_kernel(q)), pgrp_order(pgrp_image(q))];
(%o4) [4, 6]
```

See also: `pgrp_quotient`, `pgrp_kernel`

pgrp_random.summary: Returns a uniformly random element of G.
pgrp_random.body_md:
Returns a uniformly random element of `G`.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) G : pgrp_symmetric(5)$
(%i2) pgrp_member_p(G, pgrp_random(G));
(%o2) true
```

See also: `pgrp_elements`

pgrp_regular.summary: Returns G acting on its own elements by left multiplication, as in Cayley's theorem.
pgrp_regular.body_md:
Returns `G` acting on its own elements by left multiplication, as in Cayley's theorem.

Point `i` stands for the `i`-th element of `pgrp_elements(G)`.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) R : pgrp_regular(pgrp_symmetric(3))$
(%i2) [pgrp_degree(R), pgrp_order(R), pgrp_isomorphic_p(R, pgrp_symmetric(3))];
(%o2) [6, 6, true]
```

See also: `pgrp_elements`, `pgrp_isomorphic_p`

pgrp_right_cosets.summary: Returns the right cosets Hg of H in G.
pgrp_right_cosets.body_md:
Returns the right cosets Hg of `H` in `G`.

Sorted as in `pgrp_left_cosets`. For a subgroup that isn't normal, the right cosets differ from the left ones.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) pgrp_right_cosets(pgrp_symmetric(3), pgrp(pgrp_from_cycles([[1, 2]], 3)));
(%o1) [[(), (1 2)], [(2 3), (1 2 3)], [(1 3 2), (1 3)]]
```

See also: `pgrp_left_cosets`

pgrp_sign.summary: Returns 1 if p is even and -1 if it is odd.
pgrp_sign.body_md:
Returns 1 if `p` is even and -1 if it is odd.

An m-cycle is a product of m - 1 transpositions, so it is even exactly when m is odd.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) map(lambda([c], pgrp_sign(pgrp_from_cycles([c]))), [[1, 2], [1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3, 4]]);
(%o1) [- 1, 1, - 1]
```

See also: `pgrp_sign_hom`, `pgrp_alternating`

pgrp_sign_hom.summary: Returns the sign homomorphism from G onto Z_2 = {(), (1 2)}.
pgrp_sign_hom.body_md:
Returns the sign homomorphism from `G` onto Z_2 = {(), (1 2)}.

Even elements go to the identity and odd ones to (1 2), so the kernel is the even part of `G`.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) pgrp_elements(pgrp_kernel(pgrp_sign_hom(pgrp_dihedral(4))));
(%o1) [(), (1 2)(3 4), (1 3)(2 4), (1 4)(2 3)]
```

See also: `pgrp_sign`, `pgrp_kernel`

pgrp_simple_p.summary: Returns true if G is simple: not trivial, with no normal subgroups other than the trivial group and G.
pgrp_simple_p.body_md:
Returns `true` if `G` is simple: not trivial, with no normal subgroups other than the trivial group and `G`.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) [pgrp_simple_p(pgrp_alternating(5)), pgrp_simple_p(pgrp_alternating(4)), pgrp_simple_p(pgrp_cyclic(7))];
(%o1) [true, false, true]
```

See also: `pgrp_normal_subgroups`, `pgrp_composition_series`

pgrp_solvable_p.summary: Returns true if the derived series of G reaches the trivial group.
pgrp_solvable_p.body_md:
Returns `true` if the derived series of `G` reaches the trivial group.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) [pgrp_solvable_p(pgrp_symmetric(4)), pgrp_solvable_p(pgrp_symmetric(5))];
(%o1) [true, false]
```

See also: `pgrp_derived_series`, `pgrp_nilpotent_p`

pgrp_sort.summary: Sorts a list of permutations by their lists of images.
pgrp_sort.body_md:
Sorts a list of permutations by their lists of images.

Shorter permutations are compared as if padded with fixed points. Each element keeps its own form, a `pgrp_perm` value or a list.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) pgrp_sort([pgrp_perm([3, 1, 2]), pgrp_perm([2, 1, 3]), pgrp_identity(3)]);
(%o1) [(), (1 2), (1 3 2)]
```

See also: `pgrp_eq`, `pgrp_elements`

pgrp_stabiliser.summary: Returns the subgroup of G that fixes the point x.
pgrp_stabiliser.body_md:
Returns the subgroup of `G` that fixes the point `x`.

By orbit–stabiliser, the orbit of `x` times the order of its stabiliser is the order of `G`.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) S4 : pgrp_symmetric(4)$
(%i2) St : pgrp_stabiliser(S4, 4)$
(%i3) [pgrp_order(St), length(pgrp_orbit(S4, 4)), pgrp_isomorphic_p(St, pgrp_symmetric(3))];
(%o3) [6, 4, true]
```

See also: `pgrp_orbit`, `pgrp_stabiliser_chain`

pgrp_stabiliser_chain.summary: Returns the Schreier–Sims stabiliser chain of G as [k, orbit] pairs.
pgrp_stabiliser_chain.body_md:
Returns the Schreier–Sims stabiliser chain of `G` as `[k, orbit]` pairs.

Each pair is a point k and its orbit under the subgroup that fixes every point above k. The orbit sizes multiply to the order of `G`. It doesn't list elements, so it works on large groups.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) chain : pgrp_stabiliser_chain(pgrp_symmetric(4));
(%o1) [[4, [1, 2, 3, 4]], [3, [1, 2, 3]], [2, [1, 2]]]
(%i2) apply("*", map(lambda([lev], length(lev[2])), chain));
(%o2) 24
```

See also: `pgrp_order`, `pgrp_stabiliser`

pgrp_subgroup.summary: Returns the subgroup of G generated by the permutations in the list gens.
pgrp_subgroup.body_md:
Returns the subgroup of `G` generated by the permutations in the list `gens`.

Fails if a generator is not in `G`. The subgroup keeps the degree of `G`.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) H : pgrp_subgroup(pgrp_symmetric(4), [pgrp_from_cycles([[1, 2, 3, 4]])])$
(%i2) [pgrp_order(H), pgrp_degree(H)];
(%o2) [4, 4]
```

See also: `pgrp`, `pgrp_subgroups`

pgrp_subgroup_p.summary: Returns true if H is a subgroup of G.
pgrp_subgroup_p.body_md:
Returns `true` if `H` is a subgroup of `G`.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) pgrp_subgroup_p(pgrp_alternating(4), pgrp_symmetric(4));
(%o1) true
```

See also: `pgrp_normal_p`, `pgrp_member_p`

pgrp_subgroups.summary: Returns every subgroup of G, smallest first.
pgrp_subgroups.body_md:
Returns every subgroup of `G`, smallest first.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) map(pgrp_order, pgrp_subgroups(pgrp_dihedral(4)));
(%o1) [1, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 4, 4, 4, 8]
```

See also: `pgrp_normal_subgroups`, `pgrp_subgroup`

pgrp_support.summary: Returns the points that p moves, in increasing order.
pgrp_support.body_md:
Returns the points that `p` moves, in increasing order.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) pgrp_support(pgrp_from_cycles([[2, 5], [3, 4, 6]]));
(%o1) [2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
```

See also: `pgrp_fixed_points`, `pgrp_apply`

pgrp_sylow.summary: Returns a Sylow p-subgroup of G.
pgrp_sylow.body_md:
Returns a Sylow `p`-subgroup of `G`.

If the order of `G` is p^a m with `p` not dividing m, it has order p^a.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) pgrp_order(pgrp_sylow(pgrp_symmetric(4), 2));
(%o1) 8
```

See also: `pgrp_sylow_subgroups`, `pgrp_sylow_count`

pgrp_sylow_count.summary: Returns n_p, the number of Sylow p-subgroups of G.
pgrp_sylow_count.body_md:
Returns n_p, the number of Sylow `p`-subgroups of `G`.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) A5 : pgrp_alternating(5)$
(%i2) makelist([p, pgrp_sylow_count(A5, p)], p, [2, 3, 5]);
(%o2) [[2, 5], [3, 10], [5, 6]]
```

See also: `pgrp_sylow_subgroups`

pgrp_sylow_subgroups.summary: Returns every Sylow p-subgroup of G.
pgrp_sylow_subgroups.body_md:
Returns every Sylow `p`-subgroup of `G`.

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) map(pgrp_elements, pgrp_sylow_subgroups(pgrp_symmetric(3), 2));
(%o1) [[(), (2 3)], [(), (1 3)], [(), (1 2)]]
```

See also: `pgrp_sylow`, `pgrp_sylow_count`

pgrp_symmetric.summary: Returns the symmetric group S_n, generated by (1 2) and (1 2 ... n).
pgrp_symmetric.body_md:
Returns the symmetric group S_n, generated by (1 2) and (1 2 ... n).

#### Examples

```maxima
(%i1) makelist(pgrp_order(pgrp_symmetric(n)), n, 1, 6);
(%o1) [1, 2, 6, 24, 120, 720]
```

See also: `pgrp_alternating`

sections.title: Introduction to permutations
sections.body_md:
The `permutations` package adds permutation groups to Maxima, built on Robert Smith's [cl-permutation](https://github.com/stylewarning/cl-permutation). Maxima's `combinatorics` package works on single permutations. This package adds groups: order and membership by Schreier–Sims, subgroups and cosets, homomorphisms and quotients, conjugacy classes, Sylow subgroups, series, actions and counting.

**Requirements:** SBCL (Steel Bank Common Lisp). `mxpm install` fetches cl-permutation through Quicklisp.

### Quick start

```maxima
(%i1) S4 : pgrp_symmetric(4);
(%o1) pgrp(degree 4, 2 generators)
(%i2) A4 : pgrp_alternating(4)$
(%i3) [pgrp_order(S4), pgrp_order(A4), pgrp_normal_p(A4, S4)];
(%o3) [24, 12, true]
(%i4) r : pgrp_from_cycles([[1, 2, 3, 4]])$
(%i5) s : pgrp_from_cycles([[2, 4]])$
(%i6) [pgrp_compose(r, s), pgrp_compose(s, r)];
(%o6) [(1 2)(3 4), (1 4)(2 3)]
(%i7) pgrp_member_p(A4, r);
(%o7) false
(%i8) pgrp_elements(pgrp_centre(pgrp_dihedral(4)));
(%o8) [(), (1 3)(2 4)]
```

### Permutations

Results that are permutations come back as `pgrp_perm` values, shown in cycle notation, with `()` for the identity. Every function also accepts a list of images, the form the `combinatorics` package uses: `[2,1,3]` maps 1 to 2, 2 to 1 and 3 to 3. A permutation value keeps its degree, so (1 2) in S_4 has cycle type [2, 1, 1]. Equal permutations of the same degree are the same value, so `=`, `member`, `unique` and `setify` work on them; `pgrp_eq` compares across degrees. Set `pgrp_perm_output : false` to get lists of images back.

### Conventions

These follow Dummit and Foote, *Abstract Algebra*.

- Composition reads right to left: `pgrp_compose(s, t)` is s∘t, which applies `t` first. The `combinatorics` package's `permult` reads the other way.
- D_2n is the dihedral group of order 2n, generated by r = (1 2 ... n) and s, the reflection fixing vertex 1.
- Conjugates are g x g^-1, and commutators are [x, y] = x^-1 y^-1 x y.
- Actions are on the left, and `pgrp_quotient` uses left cosets.

### Limits

Most structure functions list a group's elements, so they refuse groups with more than `pgrp_max_elements` elements (100000 by default). `pgrp_order`, `pgrp_member_p`, `pgrp_orbits` and `pgrp_stabiliser_chain` don't list elements and work on groups of any size, such as the Rubik's cube group of order 43252003274489856000.

subsections.title: Permutation values
subsections.body_md: Functions return permutations as `pgrp_perm` values, shown in cycle notation. Every function also accepts a list of images, the form the `combinatorics` package uses: `[2,1,3]` sends 1 to 2, 2 to 1 and 3 to 3. A `pgrp_perm` keeps its degree, and equal permutations of the same degree are the same value, so `=`, `member`, `unique` and `setify` work on them.

subsections.title: Single permutations
subsections.body_md: Composition reads right to left, as in Dummit and Foote §1.3: `pgrp_compose(s, t)` is s∘t, which applies `t` first. This is the opposite of the `combinatorics` package's `permult`: `permult(p, q)` equals `pgrp_compose(q, p)`.

subsections.title: Named groups
subsections.body_md: The standard small groups, each as a permutation group with fixed generators.

subsections.title: Groups
subsections.body_md: A group is given by generators. `pgrp_order` and `pgrp_member_p` use cl-permutation's Schreier–Sims implementation, so they work on very large groups. Functions that list a group's elements refuse groups with more than `pgrp_max_elements` elements.

subsections.title: Actions and counting
subsections.body_md: Any finite action gives a permutation group: number the points 1, ..., n and record where each generator sends them. Burnside's lemma and the cycle index then count colourings up to symmetry.

subsections.title: Homomorphisms and isomorphisms
subsections.body_md: A homomorphism between permutation groups is fixed by the images of the generators. `pgrp_hom` checks that the images define one.

subsections.title: Subgroups and cosets
subsections.body_md: Subgroups are permutation groups of the same degree as the group they came from. Cosets are lists of permutations.

subsections.title: Quotients and conjugacy
subsections.body_md: A quotient G/N is built as a permutation group: G acting on the left cosets of N.

subsections.title: Series, Sylow subgroups and products
subsections.body_md: Series of subgroups, the Sylow subgroups, direct products and abelian groups. Except for `pgrp_stabiliser_chain`, these functions list elements, so they are limited by `pgrp_max_elements`.
